title: Choosing a President, Peruvians Familiar With Oppression and Exclusion Find Hope
author: W. T. Whitney
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/carlos-ruiz-
huaman-l91dwhigRu8-unsplash-1-680x453.jpg)

Image, Unsplash.

As the second round of presidential voting in Peru approaches on June 7, the
progressive Roberto Sánchez of the United for Justice Party is confronting
Keiko Fujimori, the right-wing candidate who has finished second in Peru’s
last three presidential elections.

First-round voting for 30 candidates took place on April 12 and extended into
the next day. Vote counting finished five weeks later, on May 17. Election
authorities
[announced](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/2026/05/17/latinoamerica/peru-jne-
proclama-resultados-fujimori-sanchez-orix) Sanchez has12.0% of the vote;
Fujimori, 17.2%; and reactionary candidate and former Lima mayor Rafael López
Aliaga, 11.9%. Only 21,000 votes separate the latter two. Flawed management by
the National Office of Electoral Processes is widely
[regarded](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/2026/05/17/latinoamerica/peru-jne-
proclama-resultados-fujimori-sanchez-orix) as scandalous.

Psychologist Roberto Sánchez won election to Peru’s Congress in 2021 and
serves there now. He had been the social development manager in Huaral
municipality, where he had run for mayor. Newly elected President Pedro
Castillo in 2021 appointed Sánchez as Minister of Foreign Trade and Tourism.
Campaigning now, Sánchez calls for a constituent assembly, support for local
economies, full access to education, reform of Peru’s large informal economy,
and community-based tourism.

Keiko Fujimori, leader of her Popular Force party, served in Peru’s Congress
(2006-2011). She is the daughter of dictatorial president Alberto Fujimori
(1990-2000), who died in 2024. She
[promises](https://www.infobae.com/peru/2026/02/23/keiko-fujimori-2026-hoja-
de-vida-estudios-experiencia-y-patrimonio-de-la-candidata-presidencial-de-
fuerza-popular/) “to confront the security crisis with an iron fist.” Degrees
obtained from Boston University and Columbia University testify to her U.S.
ties.

Fujimori gained clearance for another presidential campaign only after
judicial authorities suspended her lengthy trial in January 2025 on charges of
money laundering and illegally taking funds from Brazil’s giant Odebrecht
construction company. She had spent months intermittently in pre-trial
detention.

**Asking for trouble**

Roberto Sánchez’s situation is precarious. No progressive political movement
has achieved national political power in Peru via elections, with one
exception. Pedro Castillo won the election to the presidency in 2021. Sánchez
follows in his path.

Castillo’s enemies in Congress removed him from office in 2022. A “vacancy
vote” in Peru’s Congress led to Castillo’s dismissal and his current 11-year
prison term. Since 2016, no Peruvian president has completed a full five-year
term of office. Castillo’s enemies used legal pretexts, so-called lawfare, to
remove him. Lawfare has recently found common use throughout Latin America.

Sánchez provokes serious opposition. The public prosecutor on May 12
[announced](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/5/13/peru-presidential-
candidate-roberto-sanchez-charged-with-financial-crimes) charges against him
centering on false financial declarations relating to campaign contributions
from 2018-2020. The prosecutor is seeking Sánchez’s imprisonment for five
years, four months.

A mining-industry news outlet sounds the [alarm](https://www.mining.com/peru-
vote-uncertainty-jolts-markets-mining-sector/): “Sánchez … has pledged to
redistribute wealth to rural communities, review mining tax agreements,
rewrite Peru’s constitution and phase out open-pit mining.” Mining accounts
for 60% of Peru’s export income

A recent opinion
[poll](https://www.resumenlatinoamericano.org/2026/04/29/peru-encuesta-iep-
keiko-fujimori-es-fuerte-en-lima-pero-roberto-sanchez-gana-en-provincias)
projects Sánchez and Keiko Fujimori as winning 32% and 31%, respectively, of
the votes on June 7. Some 44% of rural Peruvians, 34% of urban voters, and 22%
of Lima residents back Sánchez. Almost [one-
third](https://www.gob.pe/en/institucion/inei/noticias/1092367-lima-supera-
los-10-millones-400-mil-habitantes) of all Peruvians live in Lima.

When Castillo – the former elementary school teacher, small farmer, and
teacher’s union leader – became president in 2021 by defeating candidate Keiko
Fujimori, he was only the second president of Peru since 1956 not to have
originated from metropolitan Lima.

**Class against class**

Sánchez promises to release Castillo from prison if he is elected president.
Receiving him on a visit, the imprisoned Castillo gave Sánchez the iconic
peasant’s sombrero he had worn as candidate and president. Sánchez, like
Castillio, receives most of his backing from “[deep](https://www.religion.uni-
bayreuth.de/en/News_Events/2023/20230626/index.html) Peru,” from the
marginalized, agrarian, and mostly mestizo or indigenous inhabitants of the
country’s central highlands.

According to one Peruvian observer, “[Since the](https://nacla.org/lumpen-
state-x-ray-peru-far-right-power/) origins of the Republic, the state has been
conceived largely as an opportunity for plunder.” Politics in Peru, until
recently, has belonged overwhelmingly to wealthy urban-based powerbrokers
oriented to neoliberalism; export income, mainly mining; and tight U.S.
relations.

Highland Peruvians in early 2024 mounted big protests against the
parliamentary coup that removed Castillo. Protests emerged both in Lima and in
southern Peru, where military
[repression](https://www.counterpunch.org/2023/03/10/indigenous-rebellion-
continues-as-post-coup-peruvian-government-flounders/) took dozens of lives,
mostly in the southeastern Puno Region. This historically excluded population
sector is solidly on Sánchez’s side.

Political struggle in Peru turns on social class disparities. Economic
inequalities are rampant. No other country matches Peru’s pattern of
[0.1%](https://ourworldindata.org/explorers/inequality?time=2022&country=COL~PER~CHL~BRA&mapSelect=COL~PER~CHL~BRA~IRQ&Data=World+Inequality+Database+%28Incomes+before+tax%29&Indicator=Share+of+the+richest+0.1%25)
of its population absorbing
[22%](https://www.resumenlatinoamericano.org/2026/04/29/peru-peru-es-el-pais-
mas-desigual-de-latinoamerica/) of all income generated in the country. Plus,
[45%](https://research-lac.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Peru-Factsheet-
US.pdf) of the country’s wealth belongs to 1% of the population. Lima may be
the country’s financial and industrial center, but [one
fourth](https://lafmnativa.com/mundiales/id-7139_La-nueva-geograf-a-de-la-
pobreza-en-el-Per-2025-por-Javier-Herrera) of Lima residents live in extreme
poverty.

In Peru now, political messaging that links class-based oppression with human
suffering is winning votes. In one department where voting favored Castillo in
2021, life expectancy was [seven years
shorter](https://www.americasquarterly.org/article/pedro-castillo-and-
the-500-year-old-lima-vs-rural-divide/) than in Lima. In another department
where he prevailed, the infant mortality rate was three times higher than in
Lima.

**Push comes to shove**

A president of Peru intent upon decent lives for the despised and excluded
underclass, like Sánchez and Castillo, is inviting major push-back –
anticommunism, to begin with.

An exchange involving Enrique Ghersi – lawyer, author, politician, and
associate of Washington’s [Cato](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Ghersi)
Institute – may be representative of the thinking of Ghersi’s Lima-based
powerbroker peers. He was being [interviewed](https://larazon.pe/enrique-
ghersi-roberto-sanchez-pondria-en-riesgo-el-crecimiento-economico-e-
inversiones/) by a prominent newspaper. Ghersi responds to a question
containing the phrase, “a communist project like that of Roberto Sánchez.” He
states that “communism is incompatible with liberal Democracy.” He declares
that Sanchez “has announced repeatedly that he seeks to reverse the economic
model that allowed for the country’s growth over decades.”

Corrective action may be on the agenda, as suggested by recent remarks from
retired General Roger Zevallos Rodríguez. [A media
report](https://www.resumenlatinoamericano.org/2026/05/04/peru-ultraderecha-
evalua-golpe-militar-si-no-gana-keiko/) appearing on May 4 alludes to a TV
interview with the general. There, he “proposed what he calls a ‘democratic
military coup’ or ‘transitional coup’ if Roberto Sánchez wins the 2026
presidential election.”

U.S. soulmates are on alert. Some have material interests determining
attitudes toward Peru. Lockheed Martin Corporation, for example, will be
selling 24 new-version F-16 fighter jets to Peru’s Air Force. Peruvian
President Dina Boluarte, Castillo’s successor, announced the deal in 2024,
along with plans for financing its $3.5 billion cost. Delivery of 12 F-16s
[takes place](https://defensearchives.com/news/peru-to-acquire-12-f-16s-from-
lockheed-martin-in-historic-1-5-billion-direct-commercial-sale/) in 2029-2030,
with 12 more being provided later on.

In late April, 2026, [José María Balcázar](https://apnews.com/article/peru-
president-congress-interim-election-c6f1e2d6c061ea8ba1cb0f4f467609bc),
president since February, [held up](https://apnews.com/article/peru-
us-f16-jets-ministers-resign-balcazar-b1df6beab04ee568dc23845d38eae0ff) the
sale, citing his lack of legitimacy as a temporary president. Peru’s defense
minister and foreign minister resigned in protest. Defense Ministry officials,
Lockheed Martin and the U.S. Ambassador ignored the president. The deal was
on.

Peru’s down-and-out majority population would have benefited from $3.5 billion
spent on their behalf. That amount in the hands of Lockheed Martin profiteers
presumably brightened their day. Booty like that appeals to U.S. capitalists
bent on extracting wealth from Peru and elsewhere. The U.S. government, on
their behalf, is ready to lend a hand in warding off social revolution. The
first step is a military presence.

U.S.-Peru agreements, from
[mid-2023](https://comunicaciones.congreso.gob.pe/noticias/aprueban-ingreso-
de-tropas-norteamericanas/) on, opened the door to annual U.S. military
deployments in Peru for months at a time;
[600](https://www.instagram.com/p/DEOQo5XTuJC/) U.S. troops served in Peru in
2025. An agreement reached in December 2025
[enabled](https://en.mercopress.com/2025/12/15/peru-grants-us-troops-access-
next-year) varying detachments to spend the entire year in Peru. President
Trump recently
[declared](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/presidential-
determination-designation-the-republic-peru-major-non-nato-ally) Peru to be a
“major non-NATO ally.”

In 2025, the two countries [determined to](https://rosalux.nyc/new-military-
enclaves-in-peru-and-ecuador/) “to build the region’s largest spaceport” at
Peru’s Talara Air Base, aided by an initial $260 million U.S. investment. In
January 2026, the U.S. government appropriated [$1.5
billion](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/americas/us-approves-15b-sale-to-upgrade-
perus-main-naval-base/3801282) to “upgrade the Peruvian Navy’s main base” at
Callao, the intention reportedly being that of confronting the new Chinese
port at Chancay, 50 miles away. For 50 years, the U.S. Navy has
[maintained](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK223706/) a biomedical
research laboratory in Lima and a smaller one in Iquitos.

The June 7 election has implications for Peru and the U.S. alike. Gustavo
Espinoza M., writer for the Marxist-oriented _Nuestra Bandera_ newspaper,
provides a [concluding
perspective](https://www.resumenlatinoamericano.org/2026/05/13/peru-en-busca-
del-golpe-de-estado/):

“[T]he local fascists … [were] certain they would win decisively in the April
12 election. …. Things didn’t go their way, and so life has pitted them
against a showdown—the one on June 7—that looks set to deliver yet another
defeat. Those who today call for a coup d’état are playing with fire. …
Roberto Sánchez and his colleagues offer … a popular, democratic, and
progressive government. Perhaps even an anti-imperialist one, insofar as they
will have to defend … the independence and sovereignty of the Peruvian state,
which is also under attack from the insatiable greed of the United States.”

The post [Choosing a President, Peruvians Familiar With Oppression and
Exclusion Find Hope](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/05/21/choosing-a-
president-peruvians-familiar-with-oppression-and-exclusion-find-hope/)
appeared first on [CounterPunch.org](https://www.counterpunch.org).
